en: Śrīḥ!

The Twelve Hymns (*Dvādaśastotra*), among all the fundamental works composed by the venerable Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda. Salutations to Śrī Lakṣmī-Hayagrīva, who is the essence of the venerable Hanumān, Abhinava-Madhva, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and Vedavyāsa.
I praise the first hymn, which extols Vāsudeva— the one worthy of worship, eternal bliss, and stainless—
who bestows boons and grants the supreme abode to Indirā and others. 1.
I bow to the lotus-feet of the Lord of Śrī, which possess a brilliance like the sun for dispelling the darkness of the heart, and whose pedestal is rubbed by the crowns of all sovereigns.
One should meditate upon the hip of the Lord, which is the support for his Jāmbūnada-gold garment,
encircled by golden anklets, and upon which the Mother of the World has ascended.
The belly of the Lord, though slender, is to be meditated upon as sustaining the entire universe;
it is eternally marked by folds and embraced by Śrī alone.
One should remember the chest of the Lord Viṣṇu, the abode of Indirā;
it is as if the infinite space has entered the space between his two arms, appearing as though it were finite.
The arms of Hari, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, should be meditated upon as thick and rounded,
constantly and solely intent on the protection of the world.
One should constantly worship the neck, which is radiant with the luster of the Kaustubha gem,
from which all the Vedas of Vaikuṇṭha are incessantly uttered.
One should remember the lotus-face of the Lord of Śrī, which possesses a splendor equal to a thousand moons, which is worthy of worship, and which dispels the distress of worldly existence.
One should always contemplate the gentle smile of Lord Govinda, which shines with the bliss of perfect non-duality and bestows the state of eternal bliss.
I remember the affectionate glance of Rāma, who is full of bliss, which bestows the nectar-ocean that destroys the torment of worldly existence. 10.
One should meditate incessantly on the knitting of the eyebrows of the Lord, which is awaited by Brahmā and the other gods,
which bestows the state of Parameṣṭhin and other realms, and which grants liberation.
I shall constantly contemplate the Infinite, especially at the time of death;
for even Brahmā and the other gods, though they recite them, have never reached the end of his qualities.
Thus ends the first hymn among the Twelve Hymns composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
May the Lord of Lakṣmī, who is the full moon for the flourishing of the ocean of virtuous people, an ocean of qualities, and dense with intense bliss, be pleased with us— this second hymn. (1)
Salutations to you, O Nārāyaṇa, who are a widow to the cakorī-bird that is Lakṣmī, a forest fire for the pride of the wicked, and a dwelling for the travelers who are the virtuous.

Salutations to Him who, having created the entire distinction between consciousness and unconsciousness and having placed [the world] therein, enjoys it; who dwells in the unmanifest cave of the heart, and who is the beloved of Ramā. || 3 ||
I bow to that Hari, who, though his essence is intense virtue, is gazed upon with a gentle smile by Indirā, and who is ever dense with bliss.
I bow to that Lord of Ramā, who is self-controlled and not subject to anyone's will, who is unconquered yet has conquered all, the creator of everything, and who is himself never created.

Salutations to you, Vāsudeva, who are beyond all qualities (aguṇa), whose essential nature is the abundance of qualities (guṇodreka-svarūpa), the primordial agent, and the one who has torn asunder the hosts of enemies.

Salutations to you, the primordial deity of the gods, the lord of the gods, the one who has destroyed all obstacles, the one who has reached the further shore of beginningless ignorance, the bestower of boons. (7)
Obeisance to you, O Garuḍa-bannered Lord, the unborn progenitor of this universe, who have conquered all the Dānavas, and whose feet are worshipful even to Brahmā and the other gods.
Salutations to the perfect Hari, whose nature is beheld by the slow and dense sidelong glances of Indirā, and who is the sole cause of our desired purpose.
Thus ends the second hymn among the Twelve Hymns composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
Perform the third hymn of praise and carry out your own prescribed duties constantly with a mind perpetually bowing at the feet of Hari;
for Hari alone is the supreme, Hari alone is the guru, and Hari alone is the refuge of the father and mother of the world. || 1 ||
There is nothing else in the world more worthy of worship than that Supreme Person, who is higher than the highest;
therefore, enough with this excessive brooding over worldly affairs—direct your mind toward the station of the Lord.
For even when one strives in the remembrance of Hari, every sin quickly goes to its dissolution;
but for one who remembers Him, the supreme state of liberation will clearly come—so why should it be warded off? (3)
Listen to these supreme words of stainless truth uttered with both arms raised in a solemn oath:
there is no one superior to Hari, nor is there anyone equal to Hari; indeed, he is beyond the entire host of conscious beings.
If indeed Hari were not supreme, how could this entire world have come under his control?
And if indeed everything were not under his control, why would he not experience eternal bliss? (5)
Nor is it the case that the body of consciousness is subject to karma, impurity, time, or the qualities (guṇas),
because there is a Vedic statement that Hari alone governs all this— the entire aggregate of both the conscious and the unconscious.
Even though there is a distinction in the conventional usage of the term "Guru" for the worlds, it does not reside in his mind, for he is not subject to being questioned.
Hari himself declared that there are many persons, yet Hari is the foremost among men.

The hosts previously liberated by the Four-faced One (Brahmā) approached Hari and, as before, always attained their own respective stations according to their fixed states of high or low status; such was the supreme word.
Hari is pleased with one who recites with devotion this *Haryaṣṭaka*, composed with devotion by the one known as Ānandatīrtha, who bears the name Pūrṇaprajña.
Thus ends the third hymn among the Twelve Hymns composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.

May the fourth hymn protect us: the Supreme Lord, whose body is immeasurable consciousness and innate, perfect bliss; the Supreme Power, possessed of infinite virtues; who is free from old age and death; the remover of all afflictions; the Lord of Kamalā; the most worthy of praise. 1.

Since Hari is blissful even when not in a state of sleep, the Vedas declare him to be the embodiment of bliss; and since the world originates from his own intellect, they call him the Lord of the Sky, whose body is supreme consciousness.

The supreme [Lord], whose power is manifold, who possesses infinite qualities, and from whom this variegated world of many forms arises—by constantly remembering His supreme state, which is of the nature of bliss, that state shall indeed belong to you. (3)
For when there is remembrance of this Lord, the All-pervading, how could the minds of beings remain defiled?
Indeed, the supreme state of the unborn Hari is stainless, self-luminous, and possesses the color of the rising sun.

Having swiftly and firmly struck down your powerful enemy— your own inner darkness— with the stainless swords of wisdom sharpened on the whetstone of the Vedas, worship the infinite Lord Hari, the destroyer of that very darkness.

For he, the most worshipful, creates, protects, and destroys others and yet others— beginning with the creators of the universe, such as Vibhu, Śambhu, Purandara, and Sūrya— and through wisdom, he leads those who bow before him to his own abode.
Even among the supreme beings, there has never been anyone equal to this Lord of Ramā, nor will there ever be;
for even in the present, no one exists who possesses a singular realization of the eternally complete and ever-countable multitude of His glories.

Thus the sage, addressed as Sukhatīrthapada, performed this supreme hymn of praise for Hari, the best of gods, with great devotion; for those who recite it, certain and exalted happiness shall surely arise. 8.
Thus ends the fourth hymn among the Twelve Hymns composed by the venerable Ānandatīrtha Bhāgavatpādācārya.
The fifth hymn:

To Vāsudeva, the immeasurable abode of nectar; to the beloved of Sundarī, who is eternally risen in purity; to the sustainer of the burden of supporting the earth; to the creator who possesses the light of fortitude.
Destroy excessive bondage; through awakening, cut away the beautiful veil. O Keśava, Keśava, Teacher, I bow to you, O Lord of the foremost heroes, worshipped by the wielder of the noose. || 2 ||
I bow to Nārāyaṇa, the stainless causeless one, the cause of causes, the perfect and most excellent;
I bow to Mādhava, Mādhava, the achiever, the destroyer of obstacles, the awakener, and the pure meditative absorption. || 3 ||
O Govinda, O Govinda, O Purandara, I bow to you whose feet are worshipped by Skanda and Sanandana;
O Viṣṇu, O Sṛjiṣṇu, O Grasiṣṇu, O Kṛṣṇa, O Saduṣṇavadhiṣṇu, O Sudhṛṣma, I worship you.
I bow to Madhusūdana, the destroyer of demons, the deity praised by the gods, whose feet are known;
O Trivikrama, you who have stepped forth, I bow to your stride, O bridge across the world, you of excellent gait, whose face utters the sound "huṃ."
O Vāmana, Vāmana, Bhāmana; I bow to Sāmana, Sīmana, Sāmana, and Sāna.
O Śrīdhara, Śrīdhara, Śandhara; I bow to Bhūdhara, Vārdhara, and Kandharadhārin.
O Hṛṣīkeśa, Sukeśa, Supreme Lord, Lord of Refuge, Lord of the Ages, Lord of Strength, Lord of Bliss;
O Padmanābha, Source of Auspiciousness, I bow to You, the Upholder of the burden of the worlds, the Supporter of the Earth.
O Dāmodara, whose inner distance is most remote, I bow to You, who have rent asunder the shoreless shore, beyond the supreme.
This *Harigīti*, composed with supreme devotion by the lord of sages, Ānandatīrtha, is like a sun for beholding the world beyond; it is most intent upon increasing devotion to Hari.
Thus ends the fifth hymn among the twelve hymns composed by the venerable Ānandatīrtha Bhāgavatpādācārya.
The sixth hymn:
O You who sport in the waters in the form of a fish, whose eyes are the Vedas, and who are praised by the four-faced Brahmā;
O You who take the form of a tortoise, who supported Mount Mandara, the sustainer of the world, and the most excellent among gods! 1.
O you who have the form of a boar, O enemy of the Dānavas, O upholder of the earth, O foremost limb of the sacrifice;
O divine Man-lion, O enemy of Hiraṇyakaśipu, O ender of all fears, O kinsman of the gods! || 2 ||

O Vāmana, O Vāmana, you who appeared in the guise of a young brahmin, the destroyer of the foremost of Daityas, whose form is the ultimate cause; O Rāma, scion of Bhṛgu’s lineage, blazing with intense splendor, the ender of the Kṣatriya clan, the most excellent of Śambhu’s boons.
O Raghava, O Raghava, enemy of the Rakshasas, beloved of Hanuman, lover of Janaki! O son of Devaki, you of beautiful form, beloved of Rukmini, kinsman of the Pandavas! || 4 ||
O son of Devakī, O prince Nanda, O ornament of Vṛndāvana, O moon of Gokula!
O you who subsist on roots and fruits, O one of beautiful form, O you whose lotus feet delight the cowherds of Gokula! 5.
O son of Indra, with Nandaka in hand, anointed with sandalwood, Lord of the beautiful women;
O Govinda, whose eyes are like the petals of the blue lotus and who bears Mount Mandara—I bow to you. 6.
O you whose face is like a hundred moons, whose smile is as pure as a kunda flower, who gladdens the gods and is full of bliss;
O deluder of the Daityas, source of eternal happiness, excellent teacher of the gods, whose very nature is that of a Buddha! 7.
O destroyer of the wicked lineages, O Kalki in essence, O increaser of Dharma, O primordial one at the beginning of the Yuga!
O Nārāyaṇa, O embodiment of pure beauty, O ocean of primal virtues, O eternally and perfectly awakened one! 8.
This auspicious song of Hari, composed by the lord of sages Ānandatīrtha, removes sin and is for the sake of eternal happiness. || 9 ||
Thus ends the sixth hymn among the Twelve Hymns composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.

I bow to that unconquered Śrī, by whose mere glance the sevenfold cosmic manifestation— consisting of dissolution, creation, great sovereignty, activity, light, restraint, bondage, and liberation— is powerfully sustained, and who is herself empowered by His side-long look.

I bow to that [Goddess] whose mere glance is inconceivable, by resorting to a fraction of whose sidelong look this entire host of gods— beginning with Brahmā, Śiva, Indra, the Sun, Dharma, and the Moon— achieves universal victory; she who is invincible through the power of her side-long glances, and who, by a mere fragment of her sidelong look, bestows all auspiciousness upon those who possess an abundance of wisdom regarding virtue, wealth, and pleasure.
I bow to the Unconquered One (Ajita), by the power of whose side-glance prosperity is irresistible, and even those who are bowed down to him with true devotion are not oppressed;
whom the sages meditate upon as Viṣṇu, having dispelled all defects through the subjugation of the six internal enemies;
and depending upon whom, even those who have come together do not experience suffering—[I bow] to that Unconquered One, by the power of whose side-glance prosperity is irresistible.

I bow to that Śrī, by the mere touch of whose sidelong glance the Creator fashions the entire universe— wondrous and vast in its arrangement of deeds, following the lead of the serpent Śeṣa, the enemy of the serpents (Viṣṇu), Śiva, and Indra—
and by the power of whose glance the Unconquered One (Viṣṇu) destroys everything, beginning with Śakra, the fierce-rayed Sun, the Moon, and the Son of the Sun (Yama).
I bow to that which is unconquerable by the power of Śrī’s sidelong glance, relying upon which Śiva—whose great power is manifest—dances;

that which has attained the state of being the great throne for the lotus-feet of Him who is more worthy of worship than Śarva and others; and relying upon the mere fraction of whose sidelong glance, the Lord of Serpents attained the sovereignty of Śrī, which is difficult for other gods to obtain. I bow to that which is unconquerable by the power of Śrī’s sidelong glance. (7)

I bow to the unconquered Śrī, whose power lies in her sidelong glances; for by resorting to even a mere fraction of her glance, the serpent-king—possessing fierce strength and prowess and endowed with supreme speed—attained the state of being Viṣṇu’s vehicle, a feat inconceivable even to the hosts of gods headed by Indra.

He who, having established this hymn—which arose from the lotus-face of the sage Ānandatīrtha, which is directly dear to the heart of Ramā’s consort, and which contains the supreme meaning—within himself, recites it with devotion, attains the desired object for both [himself and his wife].
Thus ends the seventh hymn among the Twelve Hymns composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
The eighth hymn:
To him who is the vast multitude of all those worthy of worship, whose noble and fleshy shoulders are anointed with sandalwood paste;
who is consecrated by the flickering side-glances of Lakṣmī; and whose expansive arms are like the Mandara mountain when it was being uprooted.
We gladden Vāsudeva, the peerless ornament of the circle of deities; we gladden Vāsudeva.

He who is pervaded by the playful sport of the creation and dissolution of the world, who shines with a magnificent form endowed with the six divine attributes, who is intent on the task of utterly destroying the wicked, and who is the refuge for subjects who are joyful, prosperous, and well-instructed.
We delight Vāsudeva, the peerless ornament of the circle of deities; we delight Vāsudeva.

He is the fulfiller of all that is sought by those who are uplifted, the bestower of the state of supramundane bliss upon those who bow before him, and the impeller of living beings according to their diverse karmic dispositions. Is it not thus deliberated among the wise?

We worship Vāsudeva, the ornament of the entire circle of deities; we worship Vāsudeva, who is worshipped by the foremost of Brahmins ever intent on the discourse of the Vedas, and by the most illustrious lords of the earth;
he whose qualities of vast consciousness are inconceivable, who is stainless, whose nature is luminous, undecaying bliss, and supreme.
We delight Vāsudeva, the peerless ornament of the circle of deities; we delight Vāsudeva.

He whose transgression is never known by anyone anywhere, in whose virtues the highest of men find supreme confidence, who is of true resolve, the one most excellent, the self-controlled, always proclaimed by the declarations of the Vedas with unerring words.
We delight Vāsudeva, the peerless ornament of the circle of deities; we delight Vāsudeva.
May He, who is worshipped by Brahmā and Śiva, be beheld—behold Him!—as the eradicator of the succession of sufferings for those who behold Him.
May that which is far-reaching perish, and may that which is always inherent in the self come under control by His own will, having arrived among the virtuous.
We shall please Vāsudeva, the peerless ornament of the circle of deities; we shall please Vāsudeva.
He who created the elder brother [Brahmā], whose form was the foremost of all forms, for whose very body all virtues are indeed manifest;
he who, though fierce and primordial, has as his son the most excellent offspring, and who is always well-cherished by the virtuous—he is the supreme deity.

We delight Vāsudeva, the peerless ornament of the circle of deities; we delight Vāsudeva. He who is Acyuta, eternally endowed with all virtues and forever fallen away from every defect, who is ever praised by the vast declarations of all the Vedas, and who is eternally worshipped by Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and the other gods.
We delight Vāsudeva, the peerless ornament of the circle of deities; we delight Vāsudeva.
By whom the universe, beginning with Brahmā, is always sustained; by whom the entirety of suffering is warded off for those who meditate upon him;
that which cannot be accomplished by others, yet is accomplished; and by whom all things are perpetually brought into being by all living beings.
We shall gladden Vāsudeva, the peerless ornament of the circle of deities; we shall gladden Vāsudeva.
All sins of those with purified souls go to destruction whenever they remember him with devotion;
whatever action virtuous people perform for his pleasure, it grants the status of Śiva, the Guru, and the other gods.
We please Vāsudeva, the peerless ornament of the entire circle of deities; we please Vāsudeva.
We worship Vāsudeva, the imperishable action in whom all else is established, through bowing to whom all sufferings come to an end;

we worship Vāsudeva, who is the immutable, the ageless, and eternally immortal, whose belly always contains the universe beginning with Brahmā; we worship Vāsudeva, the peerless ornament of the entire circle of deities.

We ever delight Vāsudeva—the ornament of the entire circle of deities, who is the sole adornment of the assembly of gods—He who delights the whole host of gods and others, whose broad thighs are like the banks of the Nandī river, who is himself Nandin, and who always fixes his mind upon the God of Eternal Bliss; He who bestows excellence through the corners of His eyes reddened by gentle smiles. We delight Vāsudeva.
Thus ends the eighth hymn among the Twelve Hymns composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
Ninth Hymn:
O Supreme One who destroys the delusion of excessive pride, O Source of prosperity for the Grandfather (Brahmā), O Abode of a multitude of virtues!
O You whose intention is the most auspicious discourse, O Supreme One eternally arisen, O Sole Cause of the universe, O Rāma, the Delighter of Ramā! 1.
O Lord who is eternally and beautifully worshipped by the gods through the gates of ritual action, O Beloved of Ramā’s heart, be my refuge!
O You whose intention is the most auspicious narrative, O Supreme One ever-arisen, O Sole Cause of the universe, O Rāma, O Delighter of Ramā! || 2 ||

O You whose body consists of an innumerable multitude of virtues, O You who are devoid of all that is contrary to virtue, be my refuge! O You whose intention is the most auspicious narrative, O Supreme One eternally arisen, O Sole Cause of the universe, O Rāma, the Beloved of Ramā! 3.
O you who possess a stainless and beautiful body that is an immeasurable treasury of bliss, O you whose happiness is beyond all other worldly states, be my refuge!
O Rāma, lover of Ramā, the sole cause of the world, whose intention is the most auspicious of stories, and who is eternally arisen as the Supreme! 4.
O Fish, who sport in waters where the rhythm is ever-shifting; O eternal one, consisting of bliss, be my refuge!
O Rāma, whose nature is the most auspicious narrative, eternally risen, the sole cause of the universe, the lover of Ramā! 5.
O Supreme Tortoise, who supported Mount Mandara when it was churned by the powerful Suras and Dānavas; O Bhava, be my refuge!
O Rāma, the delighter of Ramā, the sole cause of the universe, whose nature is the most auspicious narrative, and who is eternally manifest as the Supreme Being.
O Supreme Boar who supports the earth along with its mountains, O Supreme Awakening, O Bhava, be my refuge!
O Rāma, whose nature is the most auspicious narrative, eternally manifest, the sole creator of the universe, the lover of Ramā! 7.
Victory to You, O Nṛhari, who rends the hearts of those struck by exceedingly powerful [demons]; O stainless one, be my refuge!
O Rāma, lover of Ramā, the sole cause of the universe, whose intention is the most auspicious narrative, and who is eternally manifest as the Supreme! 8.

O conqueror of the sons of Bali, Mukha, and Aditi; O unconquered one who protects the world! Be my refuge, O you whose intention is the most auspicious teaching, O supreme one ever-arisen, O sole cause of the universe, O Rāma, the lover of Ramā! 9.
O Lord who has conquered the assembly of wicked kings, O destroyer of Rāvaṇa, O Consort of Ramā, O Hero, O Bhava, be my refuge!
O Rāma, whose intention is the most auspicious narrative, O Supreme One eternally arisen, O Sole Cause of the world, O Delighter of Ramā! 10.
O supreme nectar for the fire that consumes the most cruel night-stalkers, O best of the Raghus, O giver of honor, be my refuge!
O Rāma, delighter of Ramā, whose nature is the most auspicious story, who is eternally manifest, and who is the sole cause of the universe! 11.
O you of most graceful form, O giver of boons, O one of great strength, O best of the Yadus, O protector of Pārtha, be my refuge!
O you whose nature is the most auspicious narrative, O supreme one ever arisen, O sole cause of the world, O Rāma, O delighter of Ramā! 12.
O deluder of the sons of Diti, O pure awakener, O you who have awakened to the supreme virtues! O Bhava, be my refuge!
O you whose intention is the most auspicious discourse, O supremely ever-arisen, O sole cause of the world, O Rāma, lover of Ramā! 13.
O auspicious one, great festival, fire for the impurities of the Kali age, O Lord Kalkī, giver of refuge, be my shelter!
O Rāma, whose nature is the most auspicious narrative, eternally arisen, the sole cause of the universe, lover of Ramā! 14.
O cause of the dissolution of all beings, O source of supreme happiness, O Supreme Person, be my refuge!
O You whose nature is the most auspicious narrative, O eternally manifest, O sole cause of the universe, O Rāma, O lover of Ramā! 15.
Thus, O Blessed One, you who possess the highest and most constant delight in hymns of praise, be the excellent refuge for me—a sage of vast bliss;
O You whose nature is the most auspicious discourse, O Supreme One eternally arisen, O Sole Creator of the world, O Rāma, the lover of Ramā! 16.
Thus ends the ninth hymn among the Twelve Hymns composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
O Lord of Śrī, who is without equal, born from the head of Īśa and others, you who are full of compassion and the granter of boons, reveal to me your tenth hymn and your deeds. 1.
O Lord worshipped by the gods, O Excellent One, whose nature is filled with all supreme qualities;
O Compassionate Bestower of Boons, make known to me your life story. (2)
O destroyer of all darkness, O ocean of the nectar of supreme bliss,
O you who are full of compassion and bestower of boons, make your deeds known to me.
O boat for the three worlds, whose feet are always worshipped by the Lord of the gods,
who fulfills the hands [of supplicants] and grants boons— reveal Your conduct to me.
O Sustainer who transcends the three qualities, grant me pure devotion on all sides;
O Giver of Boons, reveal to me Your compassionate conduct. || 5 ||
O Father, you who are the cause of all things, be my constant refuge;
O bestower of boons, filled with compassion, reveal your deeds to me.
O protector of those at the point of death, O Lord of the universe, O bestower of boons, full of compassion, reveal to me Your deeds and Your sublime devotion.
O you whose stainless fame is like the rising sun,
O bestower of boons filled with compassion, make known your deeds to me.
O You whose high nails have the color of excellent gems with ruddy tips emerging from water, O Compassionate One, Bestower of Boons, make Your deeds known to me. (9)
O you whose power is manifested through beautiful calves resembling quivers,
O you who are full of compassion and the bestower of boons, make known your deeds to me.
O you whose supreme thighs are as firm and beautiful as the trunk of an elephant,
O you who are full of compassion and bestower of boons, make known your life-story to me.
O you whose color is like a fresh, fully blossomed flower, O ender of all obscurations, O you who are filled with compassion and bestower of boons, make known to me your conduct! 12.
O You whose navel arises from a beautiful, excellent lotus born of a hundred moons;
O Compassionate One, Bestower of Boons, reveal Your deeds to me.
O you who sprinkle the sprouts that conceal the world, O refuge for those who seek shelter, O you filled with compassion, O bestower of boons, make known to me your deeds! 14.
O Mother of the World, whose chest is the abode of the most beautiful and pure [deities], O yogi, O you who are full of compassion and bestower of boons, make known to me your life-story. 15.
O bestower of the end of the Daityas, O Lord whose excellent arms hold the discus, the conch, and the mace;
O you who are full of compassion and the giver of boons, make known your deeds to me.
O Moon-like Lord, whose face is a glorious abode for the great treasure of supreme wisdom;
O you who are full of compassion and bestower of boons, make known your life-story to me. (17)
O destroyer of the entire flood of sins, O bestower of supreme happiness upon being seen,
O you who are full of compassion and grantor of boons, make known your life-story to me.
The king of sages, Paramānanda-sutīrtha, seeking the state of supreme bliss that is eternally and perfectly full, composed this song of Hari.
Thus ends the tenth hymn among the Twelve Hymns composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
I salute the elevenfold hymn, which is exalted, undecaying, divine, and flowing with nectar; the state of bliss belonging to the Lord of the Mind, worshipped by Brahmā, Indra, and others. (1)
I bow to the supreme support of Indra, extolled by all the words of the Vedas, the state of bliss, which is worshipped by Brahmā, Indra, and the other gods.
I bow to the state of bliss belonging to the primordial god of all gods, which has rent asunder the great darkness and is saluted by Brahmā, Indra, and the other deities. (3)
I reverently and constantly salute the noble, irreproachable abode of bliss belonging to the Lord of Sindhu, which is worshipped by Brahmā, Indra, and the other gods. (4)

I salute that which resembles the interior of a blue lotus, which is perfectly full, which deludes the disputants, which is the state of bliss, and which is worshipped by Brahmā, Indra, and the other gods. (5)
O, I praise the state of bliss, which bestows the sovereignty over all immortals and liberation, and which is worshipped by Brahmā, Indra, and others. (6)
I bow to that state of bliss, worshipped by Brahmā, Indra, and the other gods, which is farther than the farthest and yet closer than the closest.

I bow to the state of bliss belonging to the Lord of the Gods, which is endowed with all perfections as its sole object, without beginning or end, and worshipped by Brahmā, Indra, and the other gods. (8)

By reciting this meritorious hymn composed by the sage Ānandatīrtha for Hari, whose nature is bliss, one shall attain bliss. Thus ends the eleventh hymn among the twelve hymns composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpādācārya.
The twelfth hymn:
O Ānanda Mukunda, whose eyes are like lotuses; O bestower of supreme bliss upon Ānandatīrtha! 1.
I praise Govinda, the abode of beauty, the bestower of supreme bliss and infinite glory. 2.
I bow to the bliss of the temple of the Moon, the bestower of supreme bliss upon Ānandatīrtha. || 3 ||
I pay homage to the one well-praised by the moon and the lord of the gods; to the bestower of supreme bliss at the shore of joy. 4.
I bow to Mandāra, Andaka, and Andana; O bestower of supreme bliss upon Ānandatīrtha! 5.
I bow to you, who are well-praised by hosts of gods, the bestower of supreme bliss upon Ānandatīrtha. 6.
I worship Mandārasyanditamaṇḍira, the supreme bliss beyond the ocean of bliss. 7.
I bow to Mandira-syandana-syandaka, the bestower of supreme bliss upon Ānandatīrtha. (8) I bow to Indirānandaka-sundara, the bestower of supreme bliss upon Ānandatīrtha. (9)
I bow to the vibration of the moonlight of bliss, O bestower of supreme bliss from the shore of bliss! 10.
Thus ends the twelfth hymn among the Twelve Hymns composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
Thus ends the twelfth hymn.
A Hymn to the Ball (A Verse on Śrī Kṛṣṇa): His feet are kissed by the celestial Gaṅgā; with the soles of His feet He shattered the massive cart;
He is the slayer of the venom of the serpent Kāliya; His eyes are as beautiful as the petals of a lotus.
May Murāri, whose body is variegated like a mass of dark clouds and who has shattered the multitudes of hundreds of enemies with hundreds of arrows,
protect us constantly— he who is devoted to the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), who possesses a speed equal to that of the wind.
Thus ends the *Kandukastuti* (The Praise of the Ball), composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda (Śrī Kṛṣṇapadya).
The virtuous Bilvamaṅgala.
May this be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Through this excellent compendium of the jewel-like works of the venerable Ānandatīrtha,
may Madhva and Mādhava— honored by Jayatīrtha and others— be pleased.
This compendium of texts was composed by Bhīmasubbārya, a disciple of Prabhañjana-sunāmin, who was born of the noble Lakṣmīrāma.
This has been offered by me, born of the lineage of Prabhañjana, who is skilled in the supreme path and possesses a beautiful voice, at the feet of Ramā and the Lord of Ramā.
